overview:
Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, a long strip of mountains and river valleys bordered by China, Vietnam, Cambodia, Thailand and Myanmar. It is about the size of Utah, and forested hills cover most of it. The Mekong, one of the great rivers of Asia, runs down the western side and forms much of the border with Thailand, carrying boats, fish and the water that fills the rice fields.

About 7.5 million people live in Laos, making it one of the least crowded countries in Asia. Lao is the official language, and dozens of other languages are spoken by ethnic groups in the highlands. Laos is a one-party socialist republic. The capital, Vientiane, is a quiet riverside city of temples and French-era buildings, while Luang Prabang upriver is a World Heritage town where saffron-robed monks walk at dawn to collect food offerings. Most families farm, above all sticky rice.
landAndNature: Forested mountains cover most of Laos, rising to Phou Bia at about 2,820 meters, and the Annamite Range walls off Vietnam to the east. The Mekong and its tributaries carry fish, boats and seasonal floods; in the south at Si Phan Don, meaning four thousand islands, the river splits into a maze of channels and sandbanks where a few rare Irrawaddy dolphins survive. The Bolaven Plateau is cool and fertile, good for growing coffee. Monsoon rains fall from May to October. Laos's forests still hold clouded leopards, gibbons and Asian elephants, and the country was once known as the land of a million elephants.
peopleAndCulture: Sticky rice is eaten with the fingers at nearly every meal, rolled into a ball and dipped into laap, a minced meat salad with herbs and lime, or into spicy green papaya salad. Most Lao are Theravada Buddhists, and many young men spend a period as monks; in Luang Prabang, lines of monks collect rice each morning from residents kneeling by the road. The khene, a bamboo mouth organ, leads lam singing, in which performers trade sung verses back and forth. Boat races on the Mekong mark the end of Buddhist Lent, and the Rocket Festival sends homemade rockets skyward to ask for rain.
history: Farming villages and bronze-working cultures date back thousands of years here, and the Plain of Jars, thousands of giant stone jars scattered across hillsides, was made about 2,000 years ago for burial rites. In 1353 the kingdom of Lan Xang, the land of a million elephants, united the region and lasted until it broke apart in the 1700s. France colonized Laos in the 1890s. During the Vietnam War, American aircraft dropped an enormous quantity of bombs on Laos to cut supply routes, making it one of the most heavily bombed countries in history; unexploded bombs still injure people and make farmland dangerous. The communist Pathet Lao took power in 1975, ending the monarchy.
funFacts: Laos is the only landlocked country in Southeast Asia, with no coastline at all.
The Plain of Jars holds thousands of stone jars, some more than two meters tall, carved about 2,000 years ago.
Unexploded bombs dropped during the Vietnam War still lie in Lao soil, and clearance teams work to remove them.
Lao families eat more sticky rice per person than anyone else in the world, shaping it into balls by hand.
The old kingdom of Lan Xang meant the land of a million elephants, a name still used for Laos today.
